How Space Waves Reveal Where Earth's Magnetic Shield Works Hardest
item.description: Earth's magnetic field is our invisible force field against the Sun's solar wind, but new research shows some patches of that shield take far more punishment than others — waves crash harder on one side than the other.

item.title: Could a planet be born from the ashes of a dead star?
item.description: Astronomers studying a dead star called a white dwarf think they may have found the first known planet born from the debris of a star's death. If confirmed, this gas-giant world would be a true second-generation planet, formed not from a stellar nursery but from the ashes of a stellar graveyard.

item.title: Europe's Sentinel-3C Satellite Shows Earth in Stunning True Color
item.description: Europe's newest Earth-observation satellite, Sentinel-3C, has beamed back its first breathtaking photos of our planet — from the snowy Alps to turquoise Caribbean waters — and is already measuring sea levels and melting ice.

item.title: How did the first stars change the universe — and where did all the elements come from?
item.description: Using the world's most powerful supercomputers, the MEGATRON project is simulating how the very first stars lit up the universe and forged the chemical elements — carbon, oxygen, iron — that make planets, pets, and people possible.

item.title: Why Does the Universe's Expansion Speed Not Add Up?
item.description: Scientists measure the universe's expansion speed two ways, but the numbers disagree — a clue from ancient cosmic magnetism might explain why.

item.title: Can a World of Melted Rock Really Keep an Atmosphere?
item.description: James Webb Space Telescope studies a super-Earth exoplanet where the ground is forever molten, yet it holds onto an atmosphere — revealing secrets about how rocky worlds, including baby Earth, keep or lose their air.

Why are the asteroid Chariklo's rings changing shape before our eyes?
item.description: Chariklo is a small asteroid with not one but two rings — and the James Webb Space Telescope has caught those rings changing right before our eyes. The inner ring is getting thicker while the outer one fades, proving that even tiny objects can host surprisingly dynamic ring systems.
